charges: Firearms offense / shooting
convicted: Yes — pleaded guilty
sentence: Arrested after a shooting during unrest following the Ferguson grand jury announcement in late 2014; court filings described shots fired from a white box truck near a crowd, a police pursuit, and a recovered revolver with spent casings. Parker pleaded guilty and received a 15-year prison sentence.

charges: Racketeering conspiracy (RICO) and related offenses
convicted: Yes — convicted at trial
sentence: Federal prosecutors alleged Cornell led the Latin Kings in Greensboro while publicly presenting as a peace advocate. After a multi-week trial he was convicted of racketeering conspiracy and related offenses and in 2013 was sentenced to 336 months (28 years) in federal prison.

charges: Conspiracy to use explosives (plot to break Oscar López Rivera out of USP Leavenworth)
convicted: Yes — pleaded guilty
sentence: Named to the FBI Ten Most Wanted list on May 22, 1987 (fugitive #411). After more than seven years underground, surrendered with partner Donna Willmott in Chicago on December 6, 1994 and was taken into custody. Charged with conspiring to use explosives to break FALN co-founder Oscar López Rivera out of USP Leavenworth; pleaded guilty.

charges: Trespass / destruction of government property (Plowshares direct action)
convicted: Yes — convicted
sentence: On August 6, 1995 (Hiroshima Day), as part of the Jubilee Plowshares/East action, Naar-Obed and partners entered Newport News Shipbuilding and boarded the USS Greenville in dry dock, pouring blood and hammering areas associated with cruise-missile capability. Arrested and prosecuted; received 12 months in federal prison. Her probation was later revoked and she was returned to federal custody in July 1999.

charges: Destruction of government property / sabotage
convicted: Yes — convicted
sentence: On April 21, 1996, Donna and Tom Howard-Hastings cut down three transmission-line poles at the U.S. Navy's Project ELF submarine-communication antenna at Clam Lake, Wisconsin (and Republic, Michigan), part of the anti-Project-ELF campaign. Each was sentenced to 3 years federal prison; Donna served 11 months before transitioning to electronically-monitored house arrest.

charges: Blockade / trespass (nonviolent direct action at Raytheon offices)
convicted: Yes
sentence: Sentenced October 14, 1999 to 30 days for blockading Raytheon corporate offices on May 28, 1999, a nonviolent action against the missile manufacturer. Released after serving the 30-day sentence.

charges: Unlawful entry / destruction of property (Plowshares direct action)
convicted: Yes — convicted
sentence: As part of a small Plowshares group, Walz entered a military aviation facility in protest, using hammers and blood as symbolic disarmament tools. Arrested and federally prosecuted; the court treated the action as criminal damage and unlawful entry and she received a prison sentence.

charges: Blockade / trespass (nonviolent direct action at Raytheon offices)
convicted: Yes
sentence: Sentenced October 14, 1999 to 30 days for blockading Raytheon corporate offices on May 28, 1999, a nonviolent action against the missile manufacturer. Released after serving the 30-day sentence.

charges: Blockade / trespass (nonviolent direct action at Raytheon offices)
convicted: Yes
sentence: Sentenced October 14, 1999 to 30 days for blockading Raytheon corporate offices on May 28, 1999, a nonviolent action against the missile manufacturer. Released after serving the 30-day sentence.

charges: Computer/telecommunications intrusion (hacking Pacific Bell systems)
convicted: Yes
sentence: Hacked Pacific Bell servers to rig radio call-in contests and reportedly uncovered evidence of FBI wiretapping; the FBI labeled him a national security risk and placed him atop its most-wanted list. Arrested in 1991 and spent about 5 years in prison.

charges: Blockade / trespass (nonviolent direct action at Raytheon offices)
convicted: Yes
sentence: Sentenced October 14, 1999 to 30 days for blockading Raytheon corporate offices on May 28, 1999, a nonviolent action against the missile manufacturer. Released after serving the 30-day sentence.

charges: Trespass and impersonation (anti-School of the Americas action)
convicted: Yes — convicted 1983
sentence: Maryknoll priest and School of the Americas Watch founder. In 1983 he was convicted on trespassing and impersonation charges linked to an anti-SOA action at Fort Benning and served 18 months in federal prison.

charges: Conspiracy (plot to free Puerto Rican nationalist prisoners; Leavenworth breakout conspiracy)
convicted: Yes — pleaded guilty
sentence: Listed on the FBI Ten Most Wanted in the 1980s as a fugitive tied to Puerto Rican independence militancy. Willmott and Claude Marks surrendered in Chicago on December 7, 1994 after years underground and were held without bail. Both ultimately pleaded guilty in connection with a conspiracy to free FALN co-founder Oscar López Rivera from Leavenworth.

charges: Destruction of government property; sabotage of nuclear missile facility
convicted: Yes — convicted in federal court
sentence: On the Hiroshima anniversary (Aug 5, 1987), Ebner and Joe Gump entered a Minuteman missile silo site near Butler, Missouri (controlled by Whiteman AFB), poured blood in the shape of a cross, and damaged electrical and alarm infrastructure before waiting to be arrested. Received a 40-month federal prison sentence.

charges: Destruction of government property; sabotage of nuclear missile facility
convicted: Yes — convicted in federal court
sentence: On Good Friday 1986 (March 28), participated in a break-in at a Minuteman missile silo site near Holden, Missouri, pouring blood and damaging the facility to protest nuclear-war preparations. Received a lengthy federal prison sentence and served multiple years, including time at Federal Prison Camp, Alderson.

charges: Destruction of government property; sabotage of nuclear missile facility
convicted: Yes — convicted in federal court
sentence: On Aug 5, 1987, Gump and Jerry Ebner entered a Minuteman missile silo site near Butler, Missouri, poured blood in the shape of a cross, and sabotaged electrical and alarm systems as a symbolic disarmament act. Received a 30-month federal prison sentence.

charges: Second-degree murder (3 counts); robbery
convicted: Yes — convicted of three counts of second-degree murder and robbery charges
sentence: Captured as the driver of a getaway vehicle after the Oct 20, 1981 Brink's armored-car robbery in Rockland County, NY. Received three consecutive 25-years-to-life sentences and served decades at Bedford Hills Correctional Facility. Gov. Cuomo commuted her sentence in 2016 to make her parole-eligible; granted parole in 2019.

charges: Murder; armed robbery (felony murder, 1981 Brink's robbery)
convicted: Yes — convicted in connection with the 1981 Brink's armored-car robbery in Nyack, NY
sentence: Convicted for his role in the Oct 1981 Brink's robbery in Nyack, NY (multiple deaths during the heist and escape). Sentenced to prison; died in custody on Dec 13, 1986 after AIDS-related illness.

charges: Conspiracy to commit mail fraud (federal); securities fraud (Virginia state)
convicted: Yes — convicted federally of conspiracy to commit mail fraud and, separately, in a Virginia state case
sentence: As a LaRouche-movement organizer/fundraiser, convicted in federal court of conspiracy to commit mail fraud and in a Virginia state case tied to fundraising described as unlawful securities-broker conduct involving solicited loans. Received a lengthy sentence in the state case and served years in prison before being paroled.

charges: Armed robbery
convicted: Yes — imprisoned prior to his political career
sentence: A former Slauson gang leader who became a revolutionary while incarcerated at the Soledad (Correctional Training Facility) prison for armed robbery in the 1960s, before founding the Southern California chapter of the Black Panther Party. Shot to death Jan 17, 1969 on the UCLA campus (a US Organization confrontation provoked by FBI COINTELPRO) — a killing, not a custody event.

charges: Attempted murder; weapons charges (indicted, later dropped)
convicted: No — indictments dropped after falsified police lab evidence was exposed
sentence: Wounded survivor of the Dec 4, 1969 Chicago police raid on Fred Hampton's apartment. Indicted with the other raid survivors; the indictments were dropped after police lab evidence was shown to be falsified.

charges: Murder
convicted: Yes — wrongfully convicted; framed via FBI COINTELPRO for a murder he did not commit
sentence: As a former Black Panther targeted by COINTELPRO, framed for a 1969 murder he did not commit and served 23 years in prison. While incarcerated (including at Green Haven) he earned graduate and undergraduate degrees and co-founded the prisoner Think Tank.

charges: Charges from a July 1969 police shootout (held under police guard)
convicted: No — died in custody before resolution
sentence: Chicago BPP member shot by police in July 1969, then held under police guard; per The Black Panther he was harassed and beaten in the hospital before dying on Sept 4, 1969.

charges: Attempted murder; weapons charges (indicted, later dropped)
convicted: No — attempted-murder and weapons indictments dropped after police lab evidence was shown to be falsified
sentence: Shot four times but survived the Dec 4, 1969 police raid on Fred Hampton's apartment. Attempted-murder and weapons indictments against him were dropped after falsified police lab evidence was exposed; he became a plaintiff in the $47.7 million civil-rights suit.

charges: Attempted murder of police officers (raid survivors)
convicted: No — indictments dropped after police lab evidence found to be falsified
sentence: Wounded and arrested in the Dec. 4, 1969 police raid on Fred Hampton's Chicago apartment. Survivors were indicted, but the charges were dropped after ballistics/lab evidence was shown to have been falsified.

charges: Murder (assassination of Malcolm X)
convicted: Yes — convicted 1966 as Thomas 15X Johnson; exonerated posthumously in 2021
sentence: Convicted of the Feb. 21, 1965 assassination of Malcolm X; sentenced to life (20 years to life). Paroned in 1987. Conviction vacated/exonerated in 2021.

charges: Murder (assassination of Malcolm X)
convicted: Yes — convicted 1966 as Norman 3X Butler; exonerated in 2021
sentence: Convicted of the Feb. 21, 1965 assassination of Malcolm X; sentenced to life (20 years to life). Paroled in 1985. Conviction vacated/exonerated in 2021.

charges: Kidnapping, murder, conspiracy
convicted: No — acquitted on all counts on June 4, 1972
sentence: Charged in the 1970 Marin County courthouse kidnapping-and-shootout because firearms used were purchased in her name. Went on the run, placed on the FBI Ten Most Wanted list, arrested in NYC on Oct. 13, 1970. Held in pretrial detention, released on bail Feb. 23, 1972, and acquitted June 4, 1972.

charges: Criminal anarchy
convicted: Yes — convicted of criminal anarchy
sentence: Arrested after the 1964 Harlem uprising for calling a rally/march in defiance of a state-of-emergency ban. Prosecuted under New York's rarely-used criminal anarchy statute; convicted and sentenced to a one-year prison term.

charges: First-degree murder
convicted: Yes — convicted of first-degree murder in 1966 at age 19; witnesses later admitted coerced testimony but a new trial was refused
sentence: Convicted of first-degree murder in Detroit in 1966 and sentenced to life. Prosecution witnesses later admitted they were coerced into lying, but Michigan refused a new trial.

charges: Illegal net fishing
convicted: Arrested and jailed for illegal net fishing during a treaty-rights 'fish-in'
sentence: Arrested in 1966 during a Nisqually-led 'fish-in' in Washington protesting restrictions that conflicted with treaty fishing rights; charged with illegal net fishing and undertook a prolonged fast while jailed.

charges: Advising/urging insubordination and refusal of duty; disloyal statements
convicted: Yes — convicted by court-martial (Dec. 1967)
sentence: U.S. Marine convicted by court-martial for privately calling Vietnam a 'white man's war'; charged with advising, urging and attempting to cause insubordination, disloyalty and refusal of duty. Sentenced to about 10 years at hard labor (combined with William Harvey's term totaling ~16 years).

charges: Blocking entrance to Armed Forces Induction Center (civil disobedience)
convicted: Arrested and jailed for blocking draft induction
sentence: Arrested in 1967 in Oakland during demonstrations at the Armed Forces Induction Center, where protesters sought to block draft processing. Served jail time as a consequence of the antiwar civil disobedience.

charges: Breach of peace (using 'whites-only' bus station facilities)
convicted: Yes — jailed for breach of peace during the Freedom Rides
sentence: Arrested in Jackson in 1961 during the Freedom Rides after entering 'whites-only' areas of the bus station and refusing to leave; imprisoned about forty days at Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman.

charges: Using contemptuous words toward officials (court-martial)
convicted: Yes — convicted by general court-martial
sentence: While off base on Nov. 6, 1965, joined an El Paso peace demonstration carrying a sign criticizing the war and the president. Convicted at general court-martial of using contemptuous words and related charges; sentenced to dismissal from the service, forfeiture of pay, and two years' confinement at hard labor.

charges: Draft evasion (Selective Service violation)
convicted: Yes — found guilty by an all-white jury in 1960; later pardoned in 2000
sentence: Refused to submit to a draft physical after the Georgia draft board addressed him by first name rather than 'Mr.' Arrested in 1960, convicted of draft evasion by an all-white jury and sentenced to 18 months. Broke bail and lived in exile abroad for decades rather than serve.

charges: Destruction of/interference with Selective Service (draft) records
convicted: Yes — convicted alongside the other Baltimore Four participants
sentence: Participated in the Oct. 27, 1967 Baltimore draft-board action, pouring blood on draft records as symbolic sabotage. Arrested and convicted with the other participants for damaging draft records and obstructing the operation of the draft.

charges: Making disloyal statements
convicted: Yes — convicted by court-martial (Dec. 1967)
sentence: Black Marine convicted in December 1967 of 'disloyal statements' for privately opposing the Vietnam War. Sentenced to about 6 years (6 to 10 years) at hard labor, held at Camp Pendleton, for words alone.

charges: Conspiracy to advocate overthrow of the government (Smith Act)
convicted: Convicted at trial in 1954; Third Circuit directed a judgment of acquittal on appeal (1957)
sentence: One of the Philadelphia Smith Act defendants. Arrested and indicted in 1953, convicted at trial in 1954. On appeal the Third Circuit found the evidence insufficient as to Weiss and directed that a judgment of acquittal be entered rather than ordering a retrial.

charges: Conspiracy to advocate overthrow of the government (Smith Act)
convicted: Convicted in 1954; conviction reversed on appeal (1957) with a new trial ordered
sentence: One of the Philadelphia Nine (also identified as David Dubensky). Arrested and indicted in 1953, convicted in 1954. In 1957 the Third Circuit reversed his conviction and held he was entitled to a new trial under the tightened legal standard for Smith Act prosecutions.

charges: Conspiracy to advocate overthrow of the government (Smith Act)
convicted: Convicted in 1954; Third Circuit directed acquittal on appeal (1957)
sentence: One of the Philadelphia Nine. Arrested and indicted in 1953, convicted with the other defendants in 1954. On appeal in 1957 the Third Circuit ruled the evidence against Katz insufficient and directed that he be acquitted.

charges: Conspiracy to advocate overthrow of the government (Smith Act)
convicted: Convicted in 1954; conviction reversed on appeal (1957) with a new trial ordered
sentence: One of the Philadelphia Nine, a Communist Party functionary tied to Philadelphia-area labor organizing. Arrested in the 1953 raids and indicted for Smith Act conspiracy; convicted in 1954. In 1957 the Third Circuit reversed the conviction and ordered a new trial for Kuzma and several co-defendants.

charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate overthrow of the government
convicted: Convicted 1954; Third Circuit reversed the conviction in 1957 and ordered a new trial, and the prosecution later collapsed
sentence: Convicted at trial in the 1953–1954 Philadelphia Smith Act prosecution of Communist Party district leadership; in 1957 the Third Circuit reversed and held Roberts (also identified as Sam Gobeloff) was entitled to a new trial under the stricter standards that followed Supreme Court narrowing of the Smith Act, and retrial became untenable
institution_name: U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Pennsylvania

charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate overthrow of the government
convicted: Convicted 1954; conviction undone and charges withdrawn in 1958
sentence: Communist Party organizational secretary for Eastern Pennsylvania and Delaware; arrested August 1953 in Massachusetts and prosecuted in the Philadelphia Smith Act case. Convicted 1954 and, unlike several co-defendants, served more than a year in federal custody at Allenwood before Smith Act limits narrowed the case and the charges were withdrawn in 1958

charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate overthrow of the government
convicted: Convicted 1954; Third Circuit reversed in 1957 and ordered a new trial
sentence: Communist Party leader in the Philadelphia region and one of nine defendants in the 1953 Philadelphia Smith Act prosecution. Convicted at trial in 1954; in 1957 the Third Circuit reversed and held Nabried and others were entitled to a new trial as courts increasingly required more than ideological association and abstract advocacy to prove conspiracy
institution_name: U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Pennsylvania

charges: Contempt of court (refusing to reveal a source)
convicted: Cited for contempt of court after refusing to reveal his source
sentence: Miami Life editor sentenced to 30 days in jail for refusing to reveal the source of leaked testimony implicating city councilman Mel Richards in accepting bribes from gambling rings; the first Florida newspaperman jailed for not revealing a source

charges: Treason
convicted: Convicted 1949 on one count of treason; granted a full pardon by President Gerald Ford in 1977, restoring her citizenship
sentence: American citizen stranded in wartime Japan who broadcast on English-language radio ('Tokyo Rose'). Arrested by U.S. occupation authorities after Japan's surrender and held about a year, then released; brought to the U.S. in 1948 for trial. Convicted 1949, sentenced to ten years and a $10,000 fine, served more than six years in federal custody (including the women's reformatory at Alderson, West Virginia), released 1956; pardoned 1977

charges: Draft refusal (violation of the Selective Service Act)
convicted: Convicted as a draft resister / conscientious objector
sentence: Poet who, after twice being rejected for enlistment, refused to serve in WWII as a matter of principle upon learning U.S. strategy included indiscriminate bombing of civilian targets; sentenced to a year and a day in federal prison

charges: Criminal syndicalism
convicted: Arrested and charged with criminal syndicalism
sentence: Daily Worker journalist arrested while covering the Harlan County coal strikes for writing sympathetically about the strikers; incarcerated four months in the Harlan County jail, threatened with lynching and held about a month in solitary confinement

charges: Armed robbery and first-degree murder (payroll robbery, two men killed)
convicted: Convicted 1921 of robbery and murder; executed by electric chair on August 23, 1927
sentence: Italian immigrant anarchist arrested in 1920 with Bartolomeo Vanzetti for a payroll robbery and the murders of two men; convicted 1921 after a highly publicized trial widely criticized as tainted by anti-radical and anti-immigrant prejudice. After years of appeals and worldwide protests, executed August 23, 1927

charges: Refusing draft registration; conspiracy (federal IWW prosecution)
convicted: Jailed after refusing draft registration in 1917, then convicted in the federal Chicago IWW conspiracy prosecution
sentence: IWW activist who in 1917 publicly refused to register for the draft and surrendered to authorities, receiving a jail sentence; later swept into the Chicago IWW conspiracy prosecution and given a multi-year federal sentence, illustrating the wartime criminalization of antiwar dissent and radical labor organizing

charges: Conspiracy (Green Corn Rebellion); draft obstruction
convicted: Convicted of conspiracy; sentenced to ten years; pardoned by President Warren G. Harding in 1921
sentence: Tenant farmer and Working Class Union organizer tied to the Green Corn Rebellion of August 2–3, 1917, an armed antiwar uprising against WWI and the Selective Service Act. Already out on bail for obstructing the 1917 draft, he was tried for conspiracy and given ten years at Leavenworth — one of the heaviest sentences on a Green Corn organizer — before Harding pardoned him in 1921

charges: Disturbing the peace
convicted: Charged with disturbing the peace; case dismissed
sentence: As spokesman for striking textile workers in Lawrence in 1919, Muste was beaten by police and jailed for about a week on an accusation of disturbing the peace before the case was dismissed

charges: Obstructing the draft (Selective Service Act)
convicted: Convicted 1917; conviction upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court
sentence: Indicted with fellow Ohio socialists (including Charles Ruthenberg and Charles Baker) for obstructing the draft during WWI; convicted 1917 and sentenced to a year, upheld by the Supreme Court, and served the term at the workhouse in Canton

charges: Refusing draft registration
convicted: Convicted for refusing draft registration during WWI
sentence: Pacifist and Christian anarchist arrested for refusing WWI draft registration and imprisoned at the federal penitentiary in Atlanta, where he led a hunger strike and spent significant time in solitary confinement — an experience he described as pivotal to his transformation

charges: Conspiracy to violate U.S. neutrality
convicted: Convicted on April 24, 1918 of conspiracy to violate U.S. neutrality
sentence: San Francisco private detective and principal field operative for the German Consulate under Consul-General Franz Bopp; a co-defendant in the Hindu-German Conspiracy trial (Nov 20, 1917 – Apr 24, 1918) accused of plots to bomb Allied munitions ships. Convicted of conspiracy to violate U.S. neutrality
institution_name: U.S. District Court, Northern District of California

charges: Conspiracy (Labor's National Peace Council munitions strikes)
convicted: Convicted of conspiracy
sentence: 'Wolf of Wall Street' stock manipulator who served as principal U.S. agent of German Naval Intelligence's Franz von Rintelen, taking about half of the $500,000 spent on the front group Labor's National Peace Council to finance strikes at U.S. munitions plants. Tried with von Rintelen in New York; after losing his appeal in 1923 he fled, was apprehended in Mexico eight months later, and served one year at the Essex County Penitentiary before his 1924 release

charges: Conspiracy to violate U.S. neutrality
convicted: Convicted on April 24, 1918 of conspiracy to violate U.S. neutrality
sentence: German Vice-Consul in San Francisco who in October 1914 approved consulate arrangements for German funds and arms shipments for an Indian uprising against British rule (Hindu-German Conspiracy). Arrested April 8, 1917 with Consul-General Franz Bopp and Wilhelm von Brincken; convicted at the Hindu-German Conspiracy trial and sentenced to two years in federal prison plus a $10,000 fine
institution_name: U.S. District Court, Northern District of California

charges: Conspiracy to violate U.S. neutrality
convicted: Convicted on April 24, 1918 of conspiracy to violate U.S. neutrality
sentence: German Consul-General in San Francisco and the most senior defendant in the Hindu-German Conspiracy trial (Nov 20, 1917 – Apr 24, 1918), which concerned the Indo-German-Irish plot to ship American arms to India and disrupt Allied munitions shipping. Directed the network via coded messages; convicted of conspiracy to violate U.S. neutrality, sentenced to two years and a $10,000 fine, and confined at the federal penitentiary on McNeil Island, Washington

charges: Conspiracy
convicted: Yes — convicted of conspiracy in federal court
sentence: German Imperial Navy officer who ran covert sabotage and strike-financing operations in the U.S. from April to August 1915. Captured by the British on his return voyage, interned, and after U.S. entry into the war extradited to the United States, tried in federal court in New York, and convicted of conspiracy. Imprisoned for three years at the Atlanta federal penitentiary.

charges: Conspiracy (WWI-era federal prosecution)
convicted: Yes — convicted in a 1917–1918 federal WWI-era prosecution; specific charges not documented
sentence: Chicago defendant convicted in a WWI-era federal prosecution and pictured in Butterick's Delineator (July 1918) gallery of Huns, Spies and Traitors, alongside the Hindu-German Conspiracy and Labor's National Peace Council defendants. Specific charges, sentence, and place of incarceration not located in available sources. Likely tried in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois.

charges: Espionage and conspiracy (U.S. criminal code §§13, 37)
convicted: Yes — espionage and conspiracy
sentence: Irish-born office clerk at the German Consulate in San Francisco; the only woman convicted in the federal Hindu-German Conspiracy trial for transmitting coded messages between Consul-General Franz Bopp and detective Charles C. Crowley. San Quentin admission record dated February 8, 1918 lists her as office clerk, age 52, birthplace Ireland.

charges: Blasphemy
convicted: Yes — convicted of blasphemy under Maine statute; conviction upheld by the Maine Supreme Judicial Court
sentence: Lithuanian-born freethought and anti-clerical lecturer prosecuted under blasphemy statutes, with a conviction in Waterbury and a later case in Rumford, Maine. After the Maine conviction was upheld by the Maine Supreme Judicial Court, Mockus left the country and lived in Mexico for several years rather than submit to imprisonment before returning to the U.S.

charges: Conspiracy (Hindu-German plot)
convicted: Yes — conspiracy to foment insurrection against British rule in India
sentence: German military attaché arrested April 8, 1917 with Consul-General Franz Bopp and Vice-Consul Eckhardt von Schack. Convicted at the Hindu-German Conspiracy trial (Nov 20, 1917 – Apr 24, 1918) and sentenced to two years in federal prison, run concurrently with a conviction for participation in bombing and dynamiting plots against Canada. Released 1920.

charges: Blasphemy
convicted: Yes — blasphemy (People v. Ruggles)
sentence: For declaring in a crowded Salem, New York tavern on Sept 2, 1810 that 'Jesus Christ was a bastard...', Ruggles was charged with blasphemy and tried in the Court of Oyer and Terminer, Washington County, on June 11, 1811. Found guilty; Justice Ambrose Spencer sentenced him to three months in prison and a $500 fine. The Supreme Court of Judicature upheld the conviction (August term 1811).

charges: Assault
convicted: Yes — convicted and fined for assault
sentence: Abolitionist reformer attacked by men attempting to forcibly shave his beard outside a Fitchburg hotel; he defended himself, was convicted of assault and fined, and when he refused to pay was imprisoned for more than a year in the Worcester County Jail.

charges: Participation in the Dorr Rebellion (Rhode Island suffrage uprising)
convicted: Detained/imprisoned for his role in the Dorr Rebellion
sentence: Labor reform speaker and suffrage agitator captured and imprisoned for his role in the Dorr Rebellion-era struggle over Rhode Island suffrage. Accounts describe an attempted escape involving setting fire to bedding before his release in 1843.

charges: Contempt of the Massachusetts General Court (seditious libel of the legislature)
convicted: Yes — convicted of contempt
sentence: Bookkeeper of the Boston Independent Chronicle, prosecuted after his brother-editor Thomas Adams over a Chronicle editorial accusing the legislature of unconstitutional conduct. Tried before Chief Justice Francis Dana of the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court in February 1799, convicted of contempt, and sentenced to thirty days in the Boston jail plus $5 in costs.

charges: Seditious libel (Sedition Act of 1798)
convicted: No — prosecution suspended after she sold the Argus and finally dropped when the Sedition Act expired in March 1801
sentence: New York publisher who took over the Democratic-Republican Argus after her husband's death. Indicted under the Sedition Act in late 1799 over articles attacking Hamilton and the Adams administration, and arrested. Prosecution suspended after she sold the paper in early 1800 and dropped after the Sedition Act expired in 1801. The only known Sedition Act prosecution of a woman publisher.

charges: Seditious libel (common law)
convicted: No — died of yellow fever Sept 10, 1798 before trial; released on $2,000 bond
sentence: Benjamin Franklin Bache, grandson of Benjamin Franklin and editor of Philadelphia's Aurora General Advertiser. Indicted under the common law of seditious libel in June 1798 for material against President Adams and the executive; arrested and released on $2,000 bond. Died of yellow fever on September 10, 1798 before he could be tried.

charges: Contempt of court
convicted: Yes — convicted of contempt in summary proceedings without a jury
sentence: Editor of the Boston Constitutional Telegraphe, prosecuted by Chief Justice Francis Dana for contempt of court in early 1801 after publishing commentary accusing Dana of judicial bias in the Abijah Adams case. Convicted in summary proceedings without a jury and sentenced to three months in the Boston jail.

charges: Seditious libel (common law and Sedition Act of 1798)
convicted: No — died in 1799 before his case could be tried
sentence: Editor and proprietor of the Boston Independent Chronicle, the leading Democratic-Republican paper in New England. Indicted by a federal grand jury in Boston in October 1798 for common-law seditious libel and again under the new Sedition Act for material attacking the Adams administration. Already gravely ill, he died in 1799 before trial; his brother Abijah Adams was prosecuted in his place.
